Why does imbalance last for months? In this lesson we cover the 2017 Barany Society diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD), symptoms made worse by upright posture, motion and visual stimuli, visual dependence, and the place of vestibular rehabilitation in a multidisciplinary approach.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Staab et al., Diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD), Journal of Vestibular Research (2017); Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management; World Health Organization, ICD-11.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, or PPPD, a common cause of imbalance that lasts for months.
We will cover the diagnostic criteria, the factors that worsen symptoms, and the place of rehabilitation in a multidisciplinary approach.
Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness is a chronic, functional vestibular disorder.
Functional dizziness is explained not by structural damage but by a change in the way the balance system works.
Nor is it a psychiatric diagnosis; the symptoms the person experiences are real and not imagined.

cumleler.yazi: The Barany Society published the criteria in 2017; PPPD is also in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases.
cumleler.ses: The Barany Society published the criteria in twenty seventeen; PPPD is also in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases.

cumleler: The definition was built from the shared features of conditions described under different names over more than thirty years.
Phobic postural vertigo, visual vertigo and chronic subjective dizziness are among these earlier concepts.
It is reported as one of the most common causes of chronic dizziness in specialized dizziness centers.
Criterion A: dizziness, unsteadiness or non-spinning vertigo is present on most days for three months or more.
Symptoms usually last for hours; they may wax and wane during the day and need not be present all day.
An important detail: in PPPD the dizziness is usually not spinning but a feeling of rocking, lightheadedness or unsteadiness.
Criterion B: symptoms are present without a specific trigger, but they get worse with upright posture, motion and visual stimuli.
Criterion C: it starts with an event causing vertigo or unsteadiness, such as a vestibular or other illness, or psychological distress.
Criterion D: the symptoms cause marked distress or impairment in daily functioning.
Criterion E: the condition is not better explained by another disease, but PPPD can coexist with other diseases.
So PPPD is not a diagnosis of exclusion; it is made with positive criteria.
The most characteristic feature of PPPD is the three factors that make symptoms worse.
The first is upright posture; symptoms increase when standing or walking and ease when sitting or lying down.
The second is motion; both the person's own movement and passive movement, as in a vehicle, make symptoms worse.
The third is visual stimuli; moving images or complex patterns clearly increase symptoms.
Supermarket aisles, crowded places, scrolling screens and patterned floors are settings people often describe.
Asking about all three factors together is the most important step in recognizing PPPD from the history.
PPPD often starts with a trigger; vestibular neuritis, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and vestibular migraine are common examples.
Panic attacks, intense anxiety, concussion and other medical illnesses can also start the condition.
In the acute phase, the brain switches to a more careful posture strategy with tight muscles to protect balance.
In the same phase it starts to rely more on visual information for balance; this is called visual dependence.
The person constantly monitors their body and surroundings, on guard; anxiety feeds this state.
Normally this emergency adaptation reverses as the triggering event passes; in PPPD it becomes persistent.
These explanations are not fully proven, but they are useful in explaining the findings and the response to treatment.
When a healthy person stands, they keep the center of mass over the base of support with small, unnoticed sways.
Meanwhile, vestibular, visual and somatosensory information are used together and flexibly.
In PPPD, the person tries to control every step carefully and holds the muscles tighter than needed.
This stiff posture disrupts normal, automatic balance control and increases the feeling of unsteadiness.
Relying too much on vision leads to a moving scene being perceived as the person's own movement.
So crowded, busy settings clearly make symptoms worse.
In PPPD, vestibular test results are often normal.
If a vestibular disease started the condition, the tests may show traces of an old, compensated loss.
But these findings alone do not explain the severity and persistence of the person's symptoms.
On examination the person may walk cautiously and stiffly; when distracted, their walking may become more natural.
Scores on self-report scales such as the Dizziness Handicap Inventory are usually high.
Normal test results do not exclude PPPD; diagnosis rests on the history and the positive criteria.
The main role of testing is to show any other vestibular problem that accompanies or started the condition.
PPPD often occurs with other conditions, and recognizing them changes the approach.
Anxiety disorders and panic attacks can be both triggers and coexisting conditions.
Depressive symptoms may accompany chronic dizziness and limit daily functioning even further.
Vestibular migraine can occur with PPPD; ask about the attacks and the ongoing unsteadiness separately.
If there is ongoing benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV, or another vestibular problem, it also needs separate assessment.
A purely example case: a forty five year old had vestibular neuritis six months ago.

cumleler: The person says symptoms get worse in the supermarket, in crowds, and when scrolling a page on a computer screen.
There is a rocking, lightheaded feeling for hours every day; sitting down brings relief.
The findings show that the old loss is compensated, but they do not explain the severity of the symptoms.
This history may fit the PPPD criteria; the findings and history are passed to the physician for diagnosis.
The approach to PPPD is multidisciplinary; a physician, audiologist, physical therapist and mental health professional may work together.
The first step is explaining the diagnosis clearly; knowing the symptoms are real and explainable is reassuring.
Vestibular rehabilitation aims at gradual habituation to the movements and visual stimuli that make symptoms worse.
Exercises start at low intensity and build up slowly; a program that is too intense can make symptoms worse.
Cognitive behavioral therapy can help reduce anxiety and avoidance behaviors.
The physician may also consider medication depending on the person's situation; this decision always belongs to the physician.
Response to treatment usually appears over weeks to months; patience and regular follow-up matter.
A person with chronic dizziness has often been to many clinics and feels misunderstood, so listening is the first step.
Normal test results can be presented as good news, showing that the inner ear and nerves are largely intact.
Explaining that the problem comes not from damage but from a change in the tuning of the balance system gives hope.
Avoid wording that suggests the symptoms are imagined or caused only by stress.
The person is told why it matters to return gradually to settings that worsen symptoms, rather than avoiding them completely.
The findings are shared with the team, and the person is referred for suitable rehabilitation and a physician's assessment.

sahneler.metin: In chronic dizziness, ask three questions: is it worse standing, worse with motion, worse in crowds and busy visual scenes?
cumleler: A tip from the field: with a complaint of dizziness lasting months, ask about each factor that makes the symptoms worse.
Is it worse when standing and walking and better when sitting, and is it worse in a vehicle or when moving?
Is it worse with visual stimuli such as a supermarket, a crowd or a scrolling screen?
If all three answers are yes, ask about the event that started it, and pass the findings to the physician so PPPD can also be considered.
In PPPD, dizziness or unsteadiness is present on most days for three months or longer.
Symptoms get worse with upright posture, motion, and moving or complex visual stimuli.
PPPD is a functional disorder; tests may be normal, but the diagnosis is made with positive criteria.
The approach includes explaining the diagnosis, graded vestibular rehabilitation, and teamwork.
